t.4.7.1: Thus addressed by the grief-stricken Rāma, the monkey Sugrīva, with joined palms, his voice choked with tears, spoke these tearful words.
t.4.7.2: I do not know at all the dwelling of that wicked rākṣasa, nor his strength or valour, nor the lineage of that base-born one.
t.4.7.3: I promise you truly: cast off your grief, O subduer of enemies. I shall make such an effort that you will win back Maithilī.
t.4.7.4: Having slain Rāvaṇa together with his host and having satisfied my own manly valour, I shall before long act in such a way that you will be pleased.
t.4.7.5: Enough of giving way to despondency; remember the fortitude that lies within yourself. Such lightness of mind is not befitting those like you.
t.4.7.6: I too have met with a great calamity, born of the abduction of my wife; yet I do not grieve like this, nor do I abandon my fortitude.
t.4.7.7: Though I am only an ordinary monkey, I do not grieve for her; how much less should you, who are great-souled, disciplined and steadfast.
t.4.7.8: You ought, through steadfastness, to hold back the tears that have welled up. You ought not to abandon fortitude, which is the bound kept by those endowed with strength of spirit.
t.4.7.9: In calamity, in financial hardship, in danger, or in peril threatening the end of life, the steadfast man, reflecting with his own understanding, does not sink into despair.
t.4.7.10: But the foolish man who constantly gives himself over to despondency sinks helplessly into grief, like a boat overladen with cargo sinking in the water.
t.4.7.11: Here, I have joined my palms in supplication; out of affection I entreat you. Resort to your manliness; you should not give grief any opening.
t.4.7.12: Those who give themselves over to grief find no happiness, and their vigor wastes away. You ought not to grieve.
t.4.7.14: Sweetly consoled by that Sugrīva, Rāghava wiped his tear-drenched face with the edge of his garment.
t.4.7.13: Tell me what is beneficial in the spirit of friendship; I do not presume to instruct you. Honoring my friendship, you ought not to grieve.
t.4.7.15: Restored to his natural composure by Sugrīva's words, the lord Kākutstha embraced Sugrīva and spoke these words.
t.4.7.16: O Sugrīva, you have done what an affectionate and well-meaning friend ought to do, and what you have done is fitting and proper.
t.4.7.17: Here I am, my friend, restored to my natural self, consoled by you; for such a kinsman is hard to find, especially at a time like this.
t.4.7.18: But you must make an effort in searching for Maithilī and for the fierce, evil-souled rākṣasa Rāvaṇa.
t.4.7.19: Speak with full confidence and tell me whatever I must do. Like seed sown in good soil during the rains, everything you wish for will come to fruition.
t.4.7.20: And this statement which I have uttered out of pride, O tiger among monkeys, let it be understood by you as the truth.
t.4.7.21: Never before have I spoken a falsehood, nor will I ever speak one. This I pledge to you; by truth itself I swear to you.
t.4.7.22: Then Sugrīva, together with his vānara ministers, was overjoyed on hearing the words of Rāghava, and especially the promise he had made.
t.4.7.23: Having heard the words of that magnanimous one, the bull among men, the monkey, foremost among the monkey heroes, wise in heart, then considered his own purpose accomplished.
